So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

#9705. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9702. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9701. 2 Supplements That Significantly Reduce Heart Disease And Cancer Risk

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

Omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil can significantly reduce heart attacks and vitamin D supplementation can significantly lower the number of deaths caused by different types of cancer.

Researchers studied 26,000 American adults in the VITAL clinical trial for five years to see if fish oil or vitamin D would definitely ward off cardiovascular disease or cancer.

The outcomes were reassuring: marine omega-3 fatty acid intake was linked to a significant drop in heart attacks.

One-and-half servings per week of dietary fish intake showed the maximum heart health benefits, but higher dietary fish intake didn’t help more.

The greatest decrease in heart attacks was seen in African-Americans.

The benefit of 1 gram of omega-3 fish oil supplementation showed a small decrease in major cardiovascular events like stroke and death from cardiovascular disease.

Vitamin D3 or cholecalciferol intake at a dose of 2000 IU per day showed a significant decrease of death from cancer for those who took it for at least two years.

However, supplementation with vitamin D3 capsules didn’t significantly lower incidence of any type of cancer or cardiovascular disease.

Dr. JoAnn Manson, the study’s first author, said:

“The pattern of findings suggests a complex balance of benefits and risks for each intervention and points to the need for additional research to determine which individuals may be most likely to derive a net benefit from these supplements.”

Dr. Stephanie Faubion, NAMS medical director, said:

“With heart disease and cancer representing the most significant health threats to women, it is imperative that we continue to study the viability of options that prevent these diseases and help women survive them.”

The 1 gram omega-3 fish oil supplementation used in the VITAL clinical trial was Omacor, a prescription medicine for adults.

The capsule contains 840 milligrams marine omega-3 fatty acids, of which 465 mg is eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and 375 mg is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

The study was presented at the North American Menopause Society (NAMS) Annual Meeting in Chicago (Manson et al., 2019).

#9699. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9694. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9693. SteamVR vient de rendre la VR plus nette. Voici ce que j'y mettrais.

Cette semaine, Valve a publié une mise à jour bêta de SteamVR qui améliore la qualité d'image transmise à tous les casques autonomes compatibles Steam Link : Meta Quest, HTC Vive Focus, PICO. Steam Link, c'est l'application de streaming de SteamVR — celle qui fait tourner votre bibliothèque Steam sans fil sur un casque autonome. La nouveauté porte sur la netteté du flux.

Vous me direz : encore une note de version. Sauf que cette note touche exactement le point qui bloquait un usage de la VR dont on parle peu.

Depuis des années, la VR se vend comme un média de jeu. Pendant ce temps, une petite communauté l'utilise pour regarder des molécules. Et cette communauté butte sur un problème très concret : lire des détails fins dans un casque. Une hélice alpha, un feuillet bêta, une chaîne latérale qui pointe vers un ligand — ce sont des objets de quelques ångströms. Si le rendu n'est pas net, la structure devient une masse colorée.

C'est un problème de pipeline, pas de puissance brute. Un flux Steam Link, c'est une chaîne : rendu côté PC, encodage, transport réseau, décodage dans le casque, reprojection. Chaque maillon ajoute sa perte. La compression vidéo lisse les arêtes fines. Le sous-échantillonnage chromatique bave sur les lignes de 1 à 2 pixels. Et une liaison peptidique, dans un rendu cartoon à distance de lecture, c'est souvent une ligne de 1 à 2 pixels. Ajoutez le mouvement de tête et la reprojection : les atomes se dédoublent dès que vous tournez.

Rien de tout cela n'est propre à la biologie structurale. Mais c'est là que ça fait le plus mal, parce que la donnée elle-même est dense. Un fichier PDB courant, c'est des milliers d'atomes, des milliers de liaisons, des feuillets superposés sur quelques ångströms de profondeur. Sur un écran 2D, on zoome et on tourne avec la souris. Dans un casque, on tourne la tête — et si l'image n'est pas stable, le cerveau décroche. La charge cognitive part dans la reconstruction de l'image au lieu de la compréhension de la structure.

Chaque amélioration de la qualité d'image rend donc une question plus crédible : et si le bon contenu pour un casque n'était pas un jeu ?

NexoPeek est un laboratoire moléculaire VR pour Meta Quest. Trois couches.

Les visites guidées. 12 visites narrées sur 6 piliers : Biotechnologie de base, Fondements de la vie, Voies et interactions, Médicaments en action, Technologies génétiques, Biotech verte. On entre dans l'hémoglobine pour voir l'oxygène se fixer. On suit le glucose qui se décompose dans la glycolyse. On regarde l'aspirine bloquer les enzymes COX. On assiste à CRISPR-Cas9 qui édite l'ADN.

Le lecteur PDB professionnel. Une recherche intelligente qui résout un nom de gène sur RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL et PDBe, et charge la structure à taille humaine. Les presets Mol* se déclenchent en un geste : cartoon, ball-and-stick, spacefill CPK, surface moléculaire, carte de facteur B, tracé en tube. Les fichiers locaux (.pdb, .cif, .mol2) s'ouvrent avec cartes de champ électrostatique et volumes de densité électronique.

Le banc d'analyse. Attraper, mettre à l'échelle, faire tourner la molécule à mains nues ou aux manettes. La prédiction de poches par IA met en évidence un site druggable (PrankWeb / P2Rank, cloud ou moteur hors ligne). Foldseek superpose un homologue. L'inspecteur de ligands trace les liaisons hydrogène et va chercher un ligand 3D dans PubChem. Deux atomes piqués, et la distance en ångströms s'affiche. Les pastilles de résidus touchées dans la séquence projettent un halo 3D sur la structure.

Et le mode Room View fait flotter la molécule dans votre pièce, menu mural toujours opérationnel.

Deux choix valent d'être explicités, parce qu'ils sont discutables.

Le premier : la recherche fédérée. On ne stocke pas de base locale. On interroge RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL et PDBe, puis on résout un nom de gène vers un identifiant de structure. Le compromis est clair — on dépend du réseau et des quotas des API publiques, mais on hérite de bases maintenues par d'autres, et on ne se retrouve jamais avec une copie périmée. Pour un outil éducatif, c'est le bon arbitrage.

Le deuxième : les presets de rendu. Mol* est puissant, mais sa surface d'API est large. On a préféré exposer des presets à un geste — cartoon, ball-and-stick, spacefill CPK, surface, carte de facteur B, tube — plutôt qu'un panneau de réglages complet. C'est une concession : on perd en expressivité ce qu'on gagne en accessibilité. Pour le public visé, ça se défend.

Côté analyse, la prédiction de poches tourne soit dans le cloud, soit sur un moteur hors ligne. Le mode hors ligne existe pour les environnements sans réseau fiable — salles de cours, labos cloisonnés. Là encore, un arbitrage : moins de modèles disponibles, mais aucune dépendance externe.

Un point sur lequel je n'ai pas de chiffres honnêtes à donner : le gain réel de la mise à jour SteamVR sur une session NexoPeek. Je n'ai pas fait de banc d'essai contrôlé, et je ne vais pas inventer un pourcentage. Ce que je peux dire, c'est que la netteté du flux est le facteur limitant côté casque autonome, et que toute amélioration de ce maillon se ressent d'abord sur les contenus denses en détails fins. La biologie structurale en fait partie.

Parce que l'actualité SteamVR n'est pas un argument de vente — c'est un signal. La VR grand public améliore lentement ce qui comptait le plus pour un usage scientifique : la fidélité visuelle. De l'autre côté, la biologie structurale produit des volumes de données que personne ne peut vraiment lire en 2D.

Ces deux courbes se rapprochent. Je pense que ça vaut la peine de le regarder de près.

NexoPeek est disponible sur le store Meta Quest : https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/

NexoPeek est un logiciel éducatif et de visualisation pour la recherche. Il ne constitue ni un avis médical, ni un diagnostic, ni un traitement. Les aides analytiques (prédiction de poches, alignement) assistent l'utilisateur et ne remplacent jamais des pipelines scientifiques validés ni le jugement professionnel.

#9692. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9689. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

IPv4 ranges use 192.0.2.0/24 / 198.51.100.0/24 / 203.0.113.0/24, and IPv6 uses 2001:db8::/32 — all of these are reserved specifically for documentation use by RFC 5737 and RFC 3849.

The key idea is to give each physical NIC a distinct role:

From an elevated PowerShell prompt, create an external switch bound to NIC2 ("Ethernet 2"):

If the switch already exists, you can apply the same setting afterward:

Add the following to %UserProfile%\.wslconfig:

This bridges WSL2 onto the WSL-LAN2 switch we just created, so WSL2 will pick up its own IP address via DHCP from the lab LAN.

It's worth making a backup copy of .wslconfig before editing it, so you can diff against it or roll back later.

Set the lab LAN's DNS server (here, as an example, 192.168.1.1) in /etc/resolv.conf inside WSL:

Check that WSL picked up an address on the lab LAN and can reach the outside world over HTTP:

#9686. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9685. Building Reliable iOS Apps With AI Agents

Senior iOS engineer at Uber. Indie app developer. 8+ years of professional experience.

Senior iOS engineer at Uber. Indie app developer. 8+ years of professional experience.

Senior iOS engineer at Uber. Indie app developer. 8+ years of professional experience.

One year ago I wrote Breaking Free from Xcode: Unlock AI's Full Potential in iOS. At that time, getting an agent to build, run and check an iOS app took a pile of MCP servers, VS Code extensions and some patience.

A lot has changed since. Models are much smarter. Xcode ships with agents built in. Claude Code can control the simulator on its own: it builds, launches, taps through screens and checks the result with screenshots.

For prototypes and MVPs, mostly yes. You can describe an idea and get the app “one-shotted”. But if your software has to be as reliable as running water (a phrase I borrow from Uber's mission: "transportation as reliable as running water, everywhere, for everyone"), two principles still matter: design and harness.

This is the biggest shift I've seen. While building a feature, I don't keep in my head which method calls which method, which file it lives in, or how state moves through each type. The agent handles that.

That doesn't mean you can stop reviewing code. Where quality matters, you still read PRs. But your attention moves up a level. You own the design of the whole system, not just one module, so architecture is now the most valuable skill you have.

At the design level you are pretty high in the hierarchy of components, that’s why visualization helps. A diagram with the right amount of detail shows how the pieces fit together, which is hard to see in plain text. The C4 model gives you that visualization at a few zoom levels.

Last year I suggested putting the project architecture in AGENTS.md. I've changed my mind: a dedicated docs/architecture/ folder is a better place. You don't need the entire architecture loaded into the context every time you do something. Instead, AGENTS.md keeps a reference to docs/architecture/context.md, so the agent can retrieve it when on demand. Luis Herrera's deep dive walks through C4 levels on a sample system.

System Context. Your app, its users and the outside systems it talks to: the backend, push notifications, analytics. This is context.md, and it links to the containers.

Containers. Conventional C4 container usually stands for a piece of software that can de deployed, like a micro-service or app. I had to adapt the original idea: a container is a feature, a flow or an SDK module, like Feed, Checkout or Networking. containers.md shows how they connect, explains what each one owns and what it may depend on, and links to components where they exist.

Components. The parts inside a container. Only draw these for complex areas, like a post composer with drafts, uploads and retries, or a sync engine. A stateless FeedService with a single getFeed() call doesn't need a component diagram. C4 itself says you only need the levels "that add value".

Code. No diagrams. Component docs just link to the specific files. The code is the source of truth, and an agent can read it faster than you can draw it.

Think about C4 as a pattern that generalizes an approach to structure progressive complexity of the architecture.

Here's what that looks like for a simple feed app:

Here's the container diagram from containers.md, as Mermaid source and rendered:

Use Mermaid. It's plain text, so it shows up in diffs, GitHub renders it, and agents read it as easily as code.

This is what I call discoverable architecture. The agent doesn't load the whole architecture up front. AGENTS.md points it to context.md, and from there it follows links down only as far as the task needs. Humans onboard the same way.

Documentation that goes stale is worse than none. So let the agent maintain it:

The script needs jq, and don't forget to chmod +x it. The stamp file matters: the docs pass runs once per new set of Swift changes, not after every question you ask.

Models are far more capable now, but they still need guidance. I regularly see agents get confused by strict concurrency and SwiftUI performance. The code compiles and the tests pass but the produced code can crash, that why your hard skills still matter.

I define these priorities in terms of resources (compute and time):

For agent review guardrails, I use skills. The most useful thing in a skill is a pair of bad and good examples. For concurrency, for example, you can show what blocking Swift's cooperative thread pool looks like:

I've caught agents writing the first version more than once and writing a linter could be an overkill or just flaky, so I put it into a skill, the review agent flags concerns when spot bad examples.

Every rule, skill and doc you add competes for the same context window, so load the right context at the right moment. Oleg Efimov explains the cost well in Navigating Claude Code: The Context Window Tax: every token you load is paid for on every turn.

Agents can write the code. What they still can't do is decide what the system should look like, or build the harness that keeps it that way. To recap:

iOS development isn't solved. The hard part has just moved up a level.

#9684. SQLPad admin and service tokens concentrate database reach

A SQL console can be more sensitive than the databases it reaches. SQLPad stores connection definitions and lets users run queries, while administrators can manage users and connections [1]. A service token created by an administrator can turn a browser convenience into a durable API credential with broad database reach.

SQLPad supports local authentication with email and password by default. Passwords are stored in its embedded database using bcrypt hashing. The initial administrator is configured through SQLPAD_ADMIN, optionally with SQLPAD_ADMIN_PASSWORD, and additional users are added by an administrator [1].

The application has two roles today, Admin and Editor. An administrator can add or edit database connections and create users. The configuration documentation says service tokens are generated by logging in as an admin and using the Service Tokens page [2]. Those tokens deserve separate review because they may outlive a browser session and are intended for automation.

I ran three count-only probes on 2026-11-09 with sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1. The application-fingerprint query app="SQLPad" matched 1,067. The title query title="SQLPad" matched 1,022. A body query http.body="SQLPad" matched 1,084.

The three counts are close, which is useful but not proof that every match is a working SQLPad instance. The app fingerprint is the strongest discovery signal in this run. The count still does not show whether authentication is enabled, which databases are connected, or who holds a service token.

Inventory every connection, its database role, network path, and owner. A SQLPad administrator may be able to edit a connection string even if they do not know the database password. The connection can use a privileged database account, so SQLPad's own role check is not the only authorization layer.

Prefer a dedicated read-only database account for analytic work. Use a separate connection for a job that needs writes. Do not let an Editor share a connection whose credentials can modify every tenant. Query-level controls, database roles, and row-level policies should remain in force.

Review the SQLPAD_USERPASS_AUTH_DISABLED and default-role settings. The documentation warns that disabling local user-password authentication can require a default role for users from another identity source [1]. A misconfigured default of Admin turns authentication success into administrative authority.

The API overview documents HTML Basic authentication for users and password access unless local authentication is disabled. Service tokens are a separate mechanism. Keep tokens in a secret manager, scope each one to a dedicated operator, and record the purpose and owner.

Test the API with a token that should be denied. Confirm that the denial is enforced by SQLPad and by the database account, not only by the UI. Review token creation and last-use records. Revoke stale tokens after integration or staff changes.

Restrict the web and API paths to a management network or a reverse proxy with strong authentication. Require TLS. Protect the embedded database because it contains password hashes, connections, and session state. Back it up with encryption and restrict restore access.

Log user, connection, query identifier, row count, and result status without storing the query text or returned data in an exposed log. Alert on queries that read unusually large volumes, connection changes, new administrators, and service-token creation.

If an administrator account is compromised, disable it, revoke its sessions and service tokens, and review connection changes. Determine which database credentials were visible and rotate them. Review the databases' own audit logs because SQLPad may not record every statement or data access.

The external SQLPad count is a discovery metric. It does not say whether a console is internet-facing, which databases are connected, or whether a token has broad authority. Review those facts at the owner, then use the count to organize outreach and follow-up.

#9683. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9681. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#9680. I gave my free D&D one-shot preview 7 days to prove itself — day 4: a sibling product closed today at zero, mine has three days left

Day 4 starts with the same numbers as day 3: 3 downloads on the Chinese PDF, 2 on the English one. Nothing moved overnight. The news today is not about this preview — it is about a sibling product that ran the same kind of test and reached its deadline first.

GitHub release asset download counts, as of 01:40 this morning (2026-11-09):

Same as yesterday morning, same as yesterday evening, same as now. The counter has not moved for anyone except me, and it did not move for me today either. Downloads from other people that I can actually prove: still zero. The 7-day target is 20 total, and the clock runs to about November 14. Both PDFs, same release:

https://github.com/alapha888/dnd-one-shot-shidu/releases/tag/trial-v1

Yesterday a different product of mine — a waitlist for a changelog-briefing tool — hit its own deadline. The rule was set in advance: 20 signups by November 9, or close it. The final count was 0 signups. Not 3, not 1. Zero.

So I closed it. The waitlist page now says validation is closed, the signup button is gone, and the entry was removed from my profile page. There was nobody to notify, because nobody had signed up.

I am writing this down because it is the same test this preview is running, and I want the record to show what the rule looks like when it bites. The preview's rule is the same shape: 20 downloads by about November 14, or stop building the full book. Right now it is at 5, and 5 includes my own checks. Three days of flat numbers is not a verdict, but it is the same shape as the line that just closed.

Nothing about the preview's numbers, and everything about how I read them. A zero at the deadline is a clean result: it says stop. A flat 5 with three days left is not yet a result, but it is no longer early either. If days 5 and 6 look like this, the honest read is the same one the sibling product got — the audience isn't there, and the full book does not get built.

Day 5 numbers tomorrow, whatever they are.

#9679. A Nasty Sign Of Omega-3 Deficiency

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

Stiffness in the joints and swelling can be indirect signs of omega-3 deficiency, research suggests.

Waking up stiff in the morning, feeling pain in the joints, swelling, tenderness and loss of flexibility are all signs of arthritis.

Omega-3 deficiency could be contributing, as scientists believe there is a link between this leading cause of disability and a lack of omega-3 in the diet.

Researchers suggest that a diet rich in omega-3 could decrease the symptoms of osteoarthritis.

A study has found that adding fish oil to the diet — and to some degree flaxseed oil (alpha-linolenic acid has an anti-inflammatory effect) — can ease or even prevent osteoarthritis.

With population aging, osteoarthritis will be one of the leading causes of disability.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, by 2040 it is estimated that 26% of US adults aged 18 or older will be diagnosed by a doctor with arthritis.

While there are still no effective medications for treating this condition, omega-3 fish oil can be one of the best natural remedies in treating osteoarthritis.

Professor John Tarlton, the lead researcher of the study, explained the effect of omega-3 on osteoarthritis:

“Classic early signs of the condition, such as the degradation of collagen in cartilage and the loss of molecules that give it shock-absorbing properties, were both reduced with omega-3.

Furthermore, there was strong evidence that omega-3 influences the biochemistry of the disease, and therefore not only helps prevent disease, but also slows its progression, potentially controlling established osteoarthritis.”

Western diets contain high levels of omega-6 fatty acids, which can lead to inflammatory disorders such as colitis, heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.

Modern diets contain up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3, whereas our ancestor’s diets contained almost an equal level of these two omega fatty acids.

Therefore, supplementation with omega-3 can help to restore this imbalance in Western diets and improve conditions such as colitis and heart-related diseases.

Fish oil is much more effective than flax seed oil, but for vegetarians and vegans this supplement is an important option.

“Most diets in the developed world are lacking in omega-3, with modern diets having up to 30 times too much omega-6 and too little omega-3.

Taking omega-3 will help redress this imbalance and may positively contribute to a range of other health problems such as heart disease and colitis.”

The study was published in the journal of Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (Knott et al., 2011).
