#9561. Add This Spicy Ingredient To Ground Beef For A Burger That's 10x Juicier

If you're looking for a burger patty that not only has a bit of kick, but also plenty of juice, you need 'nduja, a legendary Italian sausage. It is not only extremely flavorful, but also quite high in fat and moisture, making it a perfect addition no matter how you like to cook your burgers.

'Nduja is technically a type of salami, except it's far more decadent and incorporates a hefty dose of Calabrian chili peppers for next-level taste. Its high fat-to-lean meat ratio makes it perfect for introducing more moisture, even in small amounts. Even if you only have exceptionally lean meat on hand, one part 'nduja to four parts beef keeps your patties tender and juicy, and even helps develop a better crust.

The idea is similar to many meatball recipes from around the world that incorporate both pork and beef. Whereas beef provides body and a hearty texture, pork can provide extra fat, flavor, and moisture, working together to cook up something truly delicious. The peppers also create a slightly savory and spicy flavor profile that, while immediately noticeable, isn't so overwhelming that you might need to change up your preferred toppings. Each bite will drip with flavorful juices that mix with your condiments for the most moisture-rich burger possible.

Incorporating anything into a burger is a bit of a tightrope walk. You want to disperse your ingredients evenly but not work the muscle fibers so much that your patties end up dense or tough. 'Nduja's texture makes this quite easy, but you'll want to be careful about what type of meat you add it to.

Since it has a spreadable, pâté-like texture, working 'nduja directly into the meat is quite easy. Whether you mix it in thoroughly or squeeze pinches into already formed patties for pockets of flavor, you get plenty of fatty juices. Still, if you're worried about overworking your patties or want to add the salty meat at the very last minute, 'nduja is typically safe to eat right out of the package. Treat it like cheese and add a dollop after flipping your patties, letting it melt over the whole thing for a juicy entree.

If you want a custom burger blend, you have to be mindful of the proper fat-to-meat ratio. 'Nduja's exceptional fat content means it's best to add it to already lean blends so you don't end up with anything too greasy. The leaner your beef, the more 'nduja you can incorporate, so it's a balance between how much of its flavor you want included. Something that's at least 85% lean is ideal, letting you incorporate enough to taste without adding so much that you can't appreciate the beef's natural flavor.

#9560. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9559. TikToker Makes French Onion Soup In The Microwave (We Tried It, It's Legit)

French onion soup is a classic dish that has roots in ancient Roman cuisine and was further developed in France throughout the 1700s. The version we know today has ties to the city of Lyon, but it didn't get its signature toppings of toasted bread and melted cheese until it became popular in Paris. It has since become a bistro favorite and a fixture on American tables. The only problem with the soup is that even a simple recipe requires a lot of time just to caramelize the onions to perfection — around 30 minutes, at least — and one quicker alternative resorts to using a packet of instant soup mix. A TikToker, however, found a middle path that takes around 15 minutes to prepare in total.

Microwaves are efficient at heating liquids, and since raw onions contain almost 90% water, this kitchen appliance can cook them in a fraction of the time it would take on a stovetop. Starting the process in a covered bowl will sweat the onions and conserve their juices while they soften. Finishing the cooking process uncovered then evaporates those juices and allows the onions to brown.

Using beef broth or stock is also one of the best ways to add flavor to this recipe, and heating everything together for a couple of minutes melds the flavors of all the ingredients into a harmonious soup. The use of croutons is also a genius tip that cuts back on the time it would take to slice and toast a baguette. While this recipe looks legit, it almost seems too good to be true, so I decided to test it out for myself.

The beautiful thing about this recipe is that it calls for ingredients you may already have in your kitchen, and when I realized that I didn't have to make a special trip to the supermarket, I knew I had to try it out for myself. I started by slicing half an onion — we recommend using a yellow onion for the best results. Microwaving it covered for three minutes gave me the same results as in the TikTok video. However, things took a turn when I proceeded to cook the onions uncovered.

The TikToker microwaved their onions for two increments of three minutes and 30 seconds and achieved a light caramelization. My onions already reached that level of browning after the first increment of cooking, and after another minute and a half, they began to burn. Since microwave strengths vary, I recommend cooking your onions in much shorter increments to prevent the same unpleasant results. If you really want to cut back on the time and are worried about burning your onions, opt for birista, or South Asian-style crispy fried onions, that don't require cooking.

The other elements of this recipe worked beautifully, though. The addition of Worcestershire sauce added some acidity and umami to balance the deep flavors of the onions. While half a teaspoon of garlic powder may seem like a lot to add to such a small quantity of soup, it actually played well with the onions and added an additional layer of flavor to the mix. The croutons also soaked up the broth without disintegrating into the soup. I used shredded Gruyère cheese for a traditional touch, which added more dimension to the soup, but mozzarella would also work well in this recipe.

#9557. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9556. Meatloaf Is So Much Juicier When You Add This Boxed Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you want a meal that sticks to your ribs and brings a measure of comfort with every bite, you want a good, homemade meatloaf, one of America's favorite dinners. It's traditionally made with ground beef, though to keep things tender, people often include ground pork or Italian sausage. Some include a cooked-down vegetable mix to help the loaf stay moist, while others employ the use of milk. But there's a boxed (or bagged) ingredient likely already in your pantry that you might bring out next time you make meatloaf and want to avoid a crumbly, cracking mess, and it'll help create the juiciest version you've likely ever had. Instant mashed potatoes, which are great to keep on hand for soups and sauces, are about to be your secret weapon in the battle against dry meatloaf, too.

Instant mashed potatoes might sound like a strange mix-in, but hear us out. They're dehydrated and flaky, which makes them ideal when used in meatloaf because when those flakes get dampened by your other ingredients (meat, milk, egg), they thicken, adding bulk and binding the mixture together. More importantly, though, these hard-working flakes hold onto moisture, locking it inside the loaf inside instead of letting the juices run out quite so freely, so your dinner won't dry out during its long cook in the oven.

While moist meatloaf is reason enough to add instant mashed potatoes to the mix, there are a few other benefits worth considering. First and foremost: They're cheap, and they keep for a long time. You can typically get a box from Walmart for less than $4 (prices may vary), and its bags often start at just a buck apiece. Many brands can last up to a year, so you can keep them in your pantry, and they'll likely be good to go the next time you're in the mood for meatloaf (or shortcut gnocchi, for that matter).

Furthermore, most instant mashed potatoes are gluten-free. While you'll want to be sure to check the labels before using them, these potato flakes can often make meatloaf accessible to our friends and family with celiac disease or gluten sensitivities, since they can substitute for breadcrumbs.

Finally, a few tips when employing instant spuds in your dinner loaf. You might let them sit for a few minutes after combining them with the other ingredients, before you introduce the meat; this gives them the opportunity to "set up." And you're not confined to just plain buttery instant mashed potatoes. Give your supper a major upgrade with different flavors of boxed flakes, like sour cream and chives, four cheese, and more.

#9555. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

#9554. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9553. Not Butter Or Cheese: The Creamy Ingredient That Makes Grilled Cheese 10x Richer

Grilled cheese is already a decadent meal that requires little effort, but a different form of richness from meat, rather than cheese, can make it more complexly delicious. If you're going to reach for rich meat, then look no further than pâté, something that comes in enough variety to suit any cheese combination you choose for your sandwich.

Many of us are familiar with pâté on a charcuterie board, served with a light cracker so you can experience its full flavors. But it's a common sandwich ingredient — take, for example, French influence in the Vietnamese bánh mì, creating an international grilled cheese style that's as unique as it is delicious. As it heats, the pâté practically melts like a meaty butter, infusing your cheese and bread with all that richness and delivering a truly powerful taste. When done properly, the pâté should mix directly into the gooey cheese, creating a single filling with the best possible texture.

Thanks to its high fat content, pâté has a signature silky texture that's hard to find elsewhere. Even vegetarian varieties made from mushrooms, soft cheese like ricotta, and butter can be a spot of decadence on an otherwise straightforward meal. It has a remarkable capacity for taking even the most underrated cheeses and turning them into gooey perfection, even if they don't have much moisture or fat to begin with. Combined with a sturdy bread toasted with butter or mayo, each layer of your grilled cheese will end up impossibly rich.

Pâté is an extraordinarily delicate ingredient, so adding it to any hot recipe takes a bit of know-how. Some are designed to be eaten hot or cold, so selecting the right variety and application can prevent you from losing out on any of its delicious virtues. For example, a terrine — not to be confused with true pâté or even rillettes — warms beautifully.

Heating up a pâté made to be eaten cold may make it greasy and fall apart, rather than melt. Instead of these, look for ones used in pâté en croûte, a type of fluffy pastry that uses it as a filling. Just like a country variety, aka terrine, it has a coarser texture that adds a satisfying bite to your sandwich and won't split once heated. These can also come in a dizzying variety, from meaty ones seasoned with nothing but salt to ones laden with chopped vegetables, nuts, and spices.

A simple smear on one side of your bread does the trick just fine, and the direct contact with the bread lets it soak up excess fat as it heats. But if you use an aged or low-fat cheese, try incorporating it with another simple trick for a meltier result: grating the cheese first. By tossing the cheese with your pâté, you coat each individual strand with a bit of the fat and ensure that, when they melt, the two ingredients fuse together. If you use slices, it can also help to smear a bit of pâté on each one before layering them between your bread.

#9551. Grab This Packet Of Seasoning To Transform Store-Bought Snacks Into A Delicious Masterpiece

Many kitchens contain a well-stocked, if not cluttered, spice cabinet, making it easy to grab what you need when a recipe calls for spices. However, don't rule out using those jarred seasonings with store-bought snacks, too — taco seasoning is one such ideal candidate.

This savory spice blend is one of the kitchen's most versatile, useful in everything from elevating your grilled burgers to giving chicken tenders a delicious twist. Bringing together flavors like earthy ground cumin, sweet paprika, onion and chili powders, oregano, salt, and more, it's a testament to the idea that a good spice blend is greater than the sum of its parts. All the more reason to throw it on your favorite snack. Think the crunchy classics: Chex Mix, fresh or bagged popcorn, pretzels, a nut mix, or good ol' chips.

To make sure the seasoning sticks, you'll want to apply some heat and fat, not just sprinkle on the spices. Fold a packet into some tasty melted butter or coconut oil, then mix it into your snack of choice. Bake at around 350 degrees Fahrenheit, stirring occasionally, until you have a delectably browned and seasoned snack mix.

Seasonings are made for modifications. So if a simple dusting of taco seasoning isn't what you're craving, it's easy to fine-tune the flavors to your liking. An easy starting point is a sweet element — honey, agave syrup, or even maple syrup all pair fabulously with taco seasoning. Simply mix the sugary ingredient into the fat to lend the spiced mix an added dimension.

Alternatively, customize the flavors by mixing up the spice blend yourself. Taco seasoning can contain a variety of ingredients in numerous styles, so brighten up your snack seasoning with grated lime zest, or turn up the heat with cayenne or ground árbol chilies. Consider even amplifying the warmth with cinnamon or allspice — ingredients that'll pair terrifically with sweet flavors.

Alongside such reworked blends, keep expanding your store-bought snack repertoire. Throw in a bag of dry-roasted edamame beans, some Fritos, or plantain chips, or buy some chicharrones (fried pork rinds). Mix and match nibbles to your liking, dust with taco seasoning, then enjoy a new world of snackable possibilities.

#9549. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9541. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9538. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

#9536. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

#9520. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

#9519. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

#9518. Chicken with Cajun Cream Sauce

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – SO cozy! I love this meal!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 17, 2026

This was so so so good! Added into my weekly rotation!! My kids didn’t find it spicy! Big win!

That tomatoey, creamy, shallot-infused gravy is something I haven’t been able to stop thinking about.

I made this dinner for my family on the first barely chilly day a few weeks ago. I think my body had just been waiting for permission to go fall cooking mode, and I just unleashed.

Pan-fried chicken. Luscious, savory Cajun cream sauce. Homemade mashed potatoes. Green beans. Apple crisp for dessert.

I served it in deep bowls and we let the girls eat on the living room floor, using the coffee table as their table, while we watched American Ninja Warrior together with the windows open – which, frankly, is the move of two parents who are feeling extra generous and a little out of their mind with the joys of early fall weather. But that meal will be a top 5 meal for me this year, for sure. We all devoured in silence and then cozied up with full bellies to watch some ridiculous TV together.

Here’s an idea I keep coming back to: shrimp. Like what if you just made the sauce, and then threw a pound of uncooked jumbo shrimp in there? It would poach right in the sauce! I haven’t been able to pull myself away from the chicken and mashed potatoes combination, but I feel shrimp should at least be considered.

Hope this recipe gives you all same cozy fall feelings it gave me.

Also a big fan of using the air fryer here, if you’re not feeling the pan-frying.

This picture shows the shallots minced; I also really love to do this with a thinly sliced shallot, sliced on a mandoline. The shape will give you these little ribbons through the sauce.

Add cream and broth, and simmer till it’s GLORIOUS.

I mean, showstopper material right there.

My favorite combo for serving is mashed potatoes and green beans. LIGHTS OUT. So good.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – loving this easy, cozy weeknight dinner!

To air fry the chicken: Air fry at 375 for 10-12 minutes, or until at least 165 degrees internal temperature.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Oven): Toss 3-4 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt on a sheet pan. Roast the potatoes at 425 for 15 minutes. Scoot the potatoes over, add 3-4 cups broccoli and ¼ cup water to the same sheet pan, and roast for another 15 minutes.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Air Fryer): Toss 2 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt. Air fry at 375 for 12 minutes. Add 2 cups frozen or fresh broccoli; air fry at 400 for another 10-12 minutes.

Keywords: cajun chicken, chicken dinner, mashed potatoes

#9515. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

#9514. Study: Narcolepsy Medication Found to Improve Adult ADHD Symptoms

The orexin 2 receptor agonist called ALKS 7290 parallels stimulants’ path as a narcolepsy medication that evolved into an ADHD treatment.

An investigational narcolepsy medication called ALKS 7290, an orexin 2 receptor (OX2R) agonist, offers a new therapeutic approach for ADHD, according to results from a recent Phase 1B proof-of-concept study. ALKS 7290 is the first OX2R agonist to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms in adults with the condition, according to the drug’s manufacturer Alkermes plc.1

“OX2R agonists will represent an entirely new class of ADHD treatment, breaking the traditional barrier between stimulants and non-stimulant treatment,” says Greg Mattingly, M.D., a consultant on the Phase 1 and upcoming Phase 2 trials.

Stimulants remain a first-line treatment for ADHD in adults. However, not all patients tolerate the side effects of or see benefits from stimulant medications. According to an ADDitude survey of more than 11,000 adults with ADHD, 78% of respondents taking amphetamines and 70% of those taking methylphenidate experienced some side effects, compared to 66% of adults taking non-stimulant medications.

The drug works by selectively binding to and activating orexin type 2 receptors, proteins in the brain that regulate alertness, arousal, and appetite. This targeted approach could minimize potential side effects and drug misuse, according to Mattingly.

“Unlike traditional stimulants, orexin 2 receptor agonists have no direct effect on dopamine reuptake or release,” says Mattingly, Associate Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the Washington University School of Medicine. “Orexin 2 receptor agonists modulate pathways in the brain that are associated with vigilance, reward, and alertness while decreasing impulsivity. By minimizing direct effects on dopamine reuptake or release, they are considered to have a lower abuse potential.”

The two-week double-blind, parallel-group trial included 50 adults with ADHD and 88 adults without. Participants with ADHD were randomly assigned to receive ALKS 7290 at a total daily dose of 20 mg or 50 mg in split doses or placebo.

As early as day six, patients taking ALKS 7290 demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms, as measured by the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS), and in overall ADHD severity, as measured on the Clinical Global Impression-Severity Scale (CGI-S).

By day 14, treatment with ALKS 7290 reduced median baseline AISRS total scores by 14 points for the 20 mg dose and 19 points for the 50 mg dose. Median CGI-S scores declined by one point with the 20-mg dose and two points with the 50-mg dose.

ALKS 7290 was generally well tolerated at both doses, with mild side effects including insomnia, dizziness, change in sustained attention, and constipation.

The ORX2 agonist also shows promise in treating narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), a common co-occurring condition with ADHD. (Approximately 25% of people with narcolepsy have ADHD.).2 In August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Orzeyful (oveporexton), a first-in-class OX2R agonist tablet indicated to treat narcolepsy type l (NT1) in adults.3 Takeda Pharmaceuticals, Orzeyful’s manufacturer, expects the drug to be available in November 2026, pending DEA scheduling.

NT1 is a chronic sleep disorder, characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy, and sleep disruptions, resulting from a deficiency in orexin-producing neurons.4

ADHD and narcolepsy share several overlapping symptoms related to arousal and wakefulness. Before becoming standard ADHD treatment, stimulants like amphetamine and methylphenidate were used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness found in narcolepsy patients.5

“Our longest surveillance of the safety of amphetamine comes from following people with narcolepsy for their entire lives,” says ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. Today, Ritalin (methylphenidate) and Adderall (amphetamine) are both central nervous system stimulant medications approved for the treatment of ADHD and narcolepsy in adults and children.

While it is too soon to know if the OX2R agonist used to treat narcolepsy will likewise evolve into a standard ADHD treatment, the parallels to stimulant medications are clear.

“What’s exciting for clinicians was the fact that ALKS 7290 had dose-related improvement in ADHD symptoms with dramatic improvement seen early and sustained throughout the two-week study,” says Mattingly, founding partner of St. Charles Psychiatric Associates. “While preliminary, the level of improvement obtained with this molecule after two weeks was similar to what is typically seen after four to six weeks in a trial of methylphenidate or amphetamine molecules for ADHD treatment.”

Results from a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of ALKS 7290 in adults with ADHD are expected in 2027.

1 Alkermes Announces Positive Phase 1b Results Demonstrating Clinical Proof-of-Concept for ALKS 7290 in Adults With Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Press Release. September 21, 2026. Accessed October 15, 2026. https://investor.alkermes.com/news-releases/news-release-details/alkermes-announces-positive-phase-1b-results-demonstrating

2 Ren, Jiafeng, Zhao, Xianchao, Su, Changjun, et. al. (2024). ADHD in narcolepsy: A closer look at prevalence and ties. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2023.105471

3 FDA Approves First Drug to Treat the Full Range of Narcolepsy Type 1 Symptoms. Press Release. August 5, 2026. Accessed October 15, 2026. https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-treat-full-range-narcolepsy-type-1-symptoms

4 Krahn, L.E., Zee, P.C., Thorpy, M.J. (2022) Current understanding of narcolepsy 1 and its comorbidities: what clinicians need to know now. Adv Ther. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12325-021-01992-4

5 Konofal, Eric. (2024). From past to future: 50 years of pharmacological interventions to treat narcolepsy. Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pbb.2024.173804

#9513. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

This soup has become my go-to recipe when my family is sick. The broth is amazing – simple, light, flavorful, and nourishing! It’s absolute comfort food.

#9512. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9511. ADHD Lacks a Biomarker Test… But Not Scientific Validity

ADHD’s validity is confirmed not by a blood test but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence, including a reliable behavioral phenotype, genetic heritability, measurable life impairments, and more.

The diagnostic legitimacy of ADHD has been vigorously debated in contemporary psychiatry circles. For parents navigating a child’s diagnosis or adults receiving a later-in-life diagnosis, the central paradox is this: ADHD has profound, life-altering symptoms but no definitive biological test, such as a blood panel or a brain scan, to confirm its presence.

This absence of biomarkers is frequently cited by critics who characterize ADHD as a modern social construct, a byproduct of high-pressure academic environments, or a medicalization of normal childhood energy. However, the scientific consensus, codified in the 2021 World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statements, asserts that ADHD is a valid, highly heritable, and neurobiologically grounded disorder.1

In modern medicine, the gold standard for disease validation is a typically quantifiable, objective indicator of a biological state. When you are sick or injured, you expect a physician to draw blood, perform a biopsy, or order a scan or some other laboratory test. Because this reliance on objective evidence is so deeply ingrained, skeptics and critics of ADHD point to the absence of a definitive biomarker as evidence of its illegitimacy. However, these critics misunderstand (or intentionally ignore) this well-known fact: Many indisputably valid disorders cannot be affirmed with biomarker tests.

In fact, painful and disabling disorders such as migraine headaches, trigeminal neuralgia, myalgic encephalomyelitis, complex regional pain syndrome, interstitial cystitis, and mild traumatic brain injury are indisputably physical, nonpsychiatric medical diseases without biomarkers. What these critics ignore is that most, if not all, nonpsychiatric medical disorders were viewed as disorders long before a biomarker test was available.

Medical science says that we observe suffering, seek to understand its causes and treatments, and ideally, find a biomarker for diagnosis. But in the absence of a biomarker, we still must help those in need.

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

Critics of ADHD as a diagnosis also ignore the fact that psychiatric science has established criteria for what is, and what is not, a disorder. In a 2005 paper, “The Scientific Foundation for Understanding Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder as a Valid Psychiatric Disorder,” I documented how ADHD meets all these criteria.2 Below is a summary.

Does ADHD have a consistent and recognizable pattern of symptoms and functional impairments? Yes. Inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity are well defined, and those with ADHD have clear functional impairments, ranging from severe academic problems and poor peer relations to accidental injuries and occupational failure. A trait becomes a disorder when it is associated with significant distress or disability, and most people with ADHD would agree that their condition brings both.

Does ADHD have objective correlates, such as neuroimaging, psychological testing, or biochemical markers? Indeed, many studies have documented impaired performance on neuropsychological tests, small differences in brain structure and function, and genetic variants that increase risk for ADHD. This criterion does not require the correlates to be useful for diagnosis, only that they are more likely to be observed in those with the condition compared to those without.

Though individuals with ADHD are at higher risk for other disorders, the symptoms used to diagnose ADHD are different from those used to diagnose commonly coexisting disorders such as anxiety and mood disorders.

[Get This Free Download: Fight Misinformation with These 11 Facts About ADHD]

Does ADHD have a trajectory across the lifespan? Yes, the continuation of symptoms from childhood to adulthood and the emergence of other disorders associated with ADHD have been well documented.

Is there evidence of a genetic cause for ADHD? Yes, ADHD has high heritability and DNA studies show that most cases of ADHD are caused by the accumulation of many genetic risk variants.

Does ADHD have a predictable and beneficial response to specific therapeutic interventions? Yes, substantial evidence supports the benefit of stimulant and non-stimulant medications as well as parent behavior therapy for children and cognitive behavioral therapy for adults.

ADHD’s existence is undeniable. The application of these criteria to ADHD provides a rigorous scientific defense against the claim that the disorder is merely a collection of subjective labels. Its validity is established, not by a simple lab or blood test, but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence: a highly reliable behavioral phenotype, strong genetic heritability, distinct population-level neurobiological correlates, severe and measurable life impairments, and a clear response to medical and psychological treatments. Waiting for a perfect biomarker while children and adults suffer preventable harms would abandon medical responsibility.

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., is a distinguished professor of psychiatry at SUNY Upstate Medical University. He is the founder of the ADHDEvidenceProject.org.

#9509. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.

In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:

Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12

Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12

Many of the factors known to contribute to burnout are systemic and need to be addressed by health care organizations.2 However, physicians can take action to limit their stress and prevent exhaustion. The following strategies may help mitigate burnout2,4,13:

#9507. ADHD and the Social Processing Gap

“There’s a difference between having social skills and being able to use them consistently in the moment. This is the fundamental challenge for people living with ADHD.”

“Knowing social expectations versus implementing them in real time is a very big challenge for people with ADHD.” — Sharon Saline, Psy.D.

This tension is at the heart of many slip-ups — from oversharing and interrupting to difficulties reading the room — that stump adults with ADHD across various scenarios. Dr. Saline, a clinical psychologist who specializes in ADHD, described this as the “social processing gap” during her October ADDitude webinar, “Reading Body Language & Social Cues: A Primer for People with ADHD.”

Here, learn more about the gap and how to fill it, along with quick tips for navigating sticky social situations with ease and confidence.

ADHD symptoms and traits — like working memory challenges, distractibility, impulsivity, hyperfocus and more — directly impact communication and social skills. But there’s another factor that tends to influence social interactions: shame.

We asked: Which of the following social challenges prompted you to be here today — for yourself or someone important to you? (Select all that apply.)

A history of negative and uncomfortable social interactions means that many adults with ADHD approach social situations assuming they’ll misread a facial expression, take up too much of the conversation, or commit a faux pas. As a result, many are unable to fully participate in conversations without extreme vigilance and/or becoming overwhelmed, anxious, self-conscious, or exhausted.

“ADHD affects our ability to interpret social information when it’s occurring in real time, because of anxiety and rejection sensitivity that complicate those interpretations and how people respond,” Saline said.

Navigating misunderstandings in relationships, friendships, family, and work comes down to three words: Notice. Check. Clarify.

Noticing, or building social awareness, doesn’t mean scanning for signs of disapproval. It is being attuned to other people and adapting to connection, without taking things too personally or making assumptions. “The challenge is to notice these cues without automatically assuming that they’re bored, annoyed, or rejecting us,” Saline said.

That’s where clarification comes in. Uncertainty is a potent trigger for rejection sensitivity, so Saline encourages respectful questioning to address assumptions. For example, if your partner says they’re not upset but their tone sounds irritated, ask, “I’m hearing something different in your tone. Is there something you’d like to talk about?”
